content: Estonian has no grammatical gender or articles, and no separate future tense. Case endings often do the work of prepositions.
**No grammatical gender.** The pronoun **ta** can mean **he** or **she**. Estonian adjectives and verbs do not change according to gender.
Ta on õpetaja.
translation: He is a teacher. / She is a teacher.

content: **No articles.** Estonian has no direct equivalents of English **a**, **an** or **the**. Depending on context, **raamat** can mean **a book** or **the book**.

**No separate future tense.** Estonian normally uses the present tense for future events. Context or time expressions such as **homme** (tomorrow) and **varsti** (soon) tell you when something will happen.
Homme ma lähen tööle.
translation: Tomorrow I'm going to work.

content: **Case endings often replace prepositions.** English phrases such as **in town**, **from town** and **with a friend** are expressed by adding endings to Estonian nouns. Estonian also uses separate words, for example **laua peal** (on the table) and **enne tööd** (before work).
In English | In Estonian
in town | linna**s**
from town | linna**st**
with a friend | sõbra**ga**
without a ticket | (ilma) pileti**ta**
**Verbs change according to the person.** For example, ma ela**n** means 'I live', while sa ela**d** means 'you live'.
Estonian spelling is relatively consistent. Pronounce all the vowels clearly: **ema** (mother) has two distinct vowels rather than an unstressed English-style 'uh' sound.
Learn the special vowels õ, ä, ö and ü, long sounds, and the usual stress on the first syllable.
Letter | Pronunciation | Example
õ | A back, unrounded vowel [ɤ]; no close English equivalent | õde — sister
ä | Like the vowel in English 'cat' [æ] | tänav — street
ö | Rounded lips with the tongue positioned as for 'e'; similar to German ö | öö — night
ü | Rounded lips with the tongue positioned as for 'ee'; similar to German ü | üks — one
j | Like 'y' in 'yes' | jah — yes
h | Like a light English 'h' in 'hat' | hommik — morning
š, ž | 'sh' in 'ship', 's' in 'measure'; mainly in loanwords | šokolaad, garaaž
Long sounds
Double letters usually show a longer sound. Vowel or consonant length can change the meaning of a word.
Short | Long
sada — hundred | s**aa**da — to receive
tema — he, she | t**ee**ma — topic
lina — linen | li**nn**a — into town
koli — clutter | k**oo**li — to school
kala — fish | ka**ll**a! — pour!

**Estonian actually distinguishes three sound lengths:** short, long and overlong. The long and overlong forms often look identical in writing: **kooli** can be the genitive ('of the school', long) or a short illative ('to school', overlong). At first, focus on hearing the difference between short and long sounds, often written with one or two letters. Use audio to practise the finer distinction between long and overlong sounds.
Word stress
The stress is **usually on the first syllable**: **tä**nav, **õ**petaja, **ü**likool. There are exceptions, such as ai**täh** (thank you), and some loanwords.

Estonian **b, d, g** are usually pronounced with little or no voicing, closer to short, light **p, t, k** sounds than to their English equivalents. In **tuba**, the **b** is not a strongly voiced English 'b'. The letters **c, q, w, x, y** occur mainly in foreign words and names.
mina/ma, sina/sa, tema/ta… The long forms add emphasis; the short forms are common in everyday speech.

Most personal pronouns have a long and a short form. They refer to the same person. Use the short form in ordinary speech and the long form for emphasis (for example, **I**, rather than someone else).
Person | Who? (nominative) | Whose? (genitive) | Whom? (partitive)
I | mina, ma | minu, mu | mind
you (singular) | sina, sa | sinu, su | sind
he/she | tema, ta | tema, ta | teda
we | meie, me | meie | meid
you (plural/formal) | teie, te | teie | teid
they | nemad, nad | nende | neid
Person | To whom? | Who has it? | With whom?
I | minule, mulle | minul, mul | minuga
you (singular) | sinule, sulle | sinul, sul | sinuga
he/she | temale, talle | temal, tal | temaga
we | meile | meil | meiega
you (plural/formal) | teile | teil | teiega
they | neile | neil | nendega
Minu nimi on Anna. • Mu nimi on Anna.
translation: My name is Anna.

content: **teie** means 'you' when addressing several people, but it is also the polite form for addressing one person: **Kuidas teil läheb?** — How are you?
**oma** means 'one's own' and works with every person: **Ma armastan oma ema.** — I love my mother. **Ta võttis oma koti.** — He/she took his/her own bag.
**see** means 'this/that' or 'it'; **need** means 'these/those': **See on minu maja.** — This is my house. **Need on minu lapsed.** — These are my children.
To say you have something, use **mul on**: Mul on auto. For 'I don't have', use **mul ei ole**: Mul ei ole autot.
To express possession, use the **-l** form of the person or noun + **on**. The verb **on** does not change: **mul on**, **sul on**, **neil on**.
| Have | Do not have
I | mu**l** on auto | mu**l** ei ole auto**t**
you | su**l** on aega | su**l** ei ole aega
mother | ema**l** on kass | ema**l** ei ole kassi
The same pattern works with nouns. Add **-l** to the genitive stem: isa → isa**l**, õde → õe → õe**l**, sõber → sõbra → sõbra**l**.
In negative possession, the thing you do not have is in the **partitive** (the 'whom?/what?' form): auto → auto**t**, aeg → aega, raha → raha.
Mul on kaks venda.
translation: I have two brothers.

content: Mul ei ole autot.
translation: I don't have a car.

content: Kas sul on aega?
translation: Do you have time?

content: Isal on uus telefon.
translation: Dad has a new phone.

content: Use **mul on** for feelings and physical states, too
Mul on külm. • Mul on palav.
translation: I'm cold. • I'm hot.

content: Mul on hea meel.
translation: I'm happy. / I'm glad.

content: Mul on vaja minna.
translation: I need to go.

content: Mul on kõht tühi.
translation: I'm hungry.

content: Learn common **mul on** expressions as complete phrases. Their natural English translations often use **I am** or **I need**, not **I have**.
Incorrect: “Mul ei ole auto.” In negative possession, the noun must be partitive: Mul ei ole auto**t**.
In everyday Estonian, **pole** often replaces **ei ole**: **Mul pole aega.** — I don't have time.
kes, mis, kus, kuhu, kust, millal, miks, kuidas, mitu, kui palju…
Question word | Meaning | Example
kes? | who? | Kes see on?
mis? | what? which? | Mis see on?
kus? | where? (location) | Kus sa elad?
kuhu? | where to? | Kuhu sa lähed?
kust? | where from? | Kust sa tuled?
millal? | when? | Millal buss tuleb?
mis kell? | at what time? | Mis kell film algab?
miks? | why? | Miks sa naerad?
kuidas? | how? | Kuidas läheb?
mitu? | how many? (countable items) | Mitu last sul on?
kui palju? | how much? how many? | Kui palju see maksab?
milline? missugune? | what kind of? which? | Milline ilm täna on?
kelle? | whose? | Kelle kott see on?
keda? | whom? | Keda sa ootad?
mida? | what? (object) | Mida sa soovid?
kellega? | with whom? | Kellega sa räägid?
Questions and answers
Kus sa elad? — Ma elan Tallinnas.
translation: Where do you live? — I live in Tallinn.

content: Kuhu sa lähed? — Poodi.
translation: Where are you going? — To the shop.

content: Kust sa tuled? — Töölt.
translation: Where are you coming from? — From work.

content: Mitu last sul on? — Kaks.
translation: How many children do you have? — Two.

content: Kui palju see maksab? — Viis eurot.
translation: How much does it cost? — Five euros.

content: Mis kell rong läheb? — Kell kaheksa.

content: Kelle telefon see on? — Minu.

content: **kus / kuhu / kust** help you choose the location form in the answer: **kus?** (where?) → **-s** or **-l** (poes, tööl); **kuhu?** (where to?) → **-sse** or **-le**, or a short form (poodi, tööle); **kust?** (where from?) → **-st** or **-lt** (poest, töölt).

**mitu?** asks how many countable items there are. It takes the **singular partitive**: **mitu last? mitu piletit?** **kui palju?** asks about quantity or amount: **kui palju aega? kui palju raha?** With countable nouns after **kui palju**, use the plural partitive: **kui palju inimesi?**
In everyday speech, **mis?** can also mean 'what kind of?' or 'which?': **Mis värvi on su auto?** — What colour is your car? **milline?** and **missugune?** ask which one or what kind.
**Kas sa räägid eesti keelt?** — **Jah, räägin. / Ei, ei räägi.** Use **kas** to ask a yes/no question.
A yes/no question usually begins with **kas**. The rest of the word order stays the same as in a statement.
Sa räägid eesti keelt. → Kas sa räägid eesti keelt?
translation: You speak Estonian. → Do you speak Estonian?

content: In a short answer, repeat the verb: **jah** (yes) + the verb, or **ei** (no) + the negative verb form.
Kas sa räägid eesti keelt? — Jah, räägin. • Ei, ei räägi.
translation: Do you speak Estonian? — Yes, I do. • No, I don't.

content: Kas sul on aega? — Jah, on. • Ei ole.
translation: Do you have time? — Yes, I do. • No, I don't.

content: Kas see on sinu kott? — Jah, minu.
translation: Is this your bag? — Yes, it's mine.

content: Kas kohvi või teed?
translation: Coffee or tea?

content: When a question already contains a question word such as **kus**, **mis** or **kes**, you do not need **kas**: **Kus sa elad?** In casual conversation, speakers may also leave out **kas** and signal a yes/no question through intonation.
Present-tense forms include **ma olen, sa oled, ta on, me oleme, te olete, nad on**. The verb 'to be' is normally expressed in Estonian, just as it is in English.
Person | Affirmative | Negative
I | ma ole**n** | ma ei ole
you (singular) | sa ole**d** | sa ei ole
he/she | ta **on** | ta ei ole
we | me ole**me** | me ei ole
you (plural/formal) | te ole**te** | te ei ole
they | nad **on** | nad ei ole
**Olema** means 'to be'. It is generally required when identifying or describing someone: **Ma olen õpetaja.** — I am a teacher.
Incorrect: **Ma õpetaja.** You need the verb **olen**: **Ma olen õpetaja.**
Ma olen õpetaja.
translation: I am a teacher.

content: Ta on kodus.
translation: He/she is at home.

content: Me oleme Tallinnas.
translation: We are in Tallinn.

content: See on hea.
translation: This is good.

content: Siin on pood.

content: Ma ei ole väsinud.
translation: I am not tired.

content: Simple past: **ma olin** (I was), **ta oli** (he/she was), **nad olid** (they were). Negative: **ma ei olnud** (I was not). In everyday speech, **ei ole** is often shortened to **pole**.
Present-tense endings: **-n, -d, -b, -me, -te, -vad**: ma elan, sa elad, ta elab…
Add a personal ending to the verb stem. The endings are the same for most verbs. A notable exception is **olema**: **ta on**, **nad on**.
Person | Ending | elama — to live | õppima — to study, learn
ma | -n | ela**n** | õpi**n**
sa | -d | ela**d** | õpi**d**
ta | -b | ela**b** | õpi**b**
me | -me | ela**me** | õpi**me**
te | -te | ela**te** | õpi**te**
nad | -vad | ela**vad** | õpi**vad**
The stem often changes: **õppima → ma õpin, lugema → ma loen, rääkima → ma räägin**. It helps to learn the 'I' form with every verb: **lugema — loen**.
Verb | I | he/she | they
tegema — to do, make | teen | teeb | teevad
minema — to go | lähen | läheb | lähevad
lugema — to read | loen | loeb | loevad
nägema — to see | näen | näeb | näevad
sööma — to eat | söön | sööb | söövad
jooma — to drink | joon | joob | joovad
Ma elan Tallinnas.
translation: I live in Tallinn.

content: The present tense can also refer to the future: **Homme ma töötan kodus.** — I'll work from home tomorrow.
**ei** + the verb stem without a personal ending: **ma ei tea**, **nad ei tea**. The negative form is the same for every person.
To make a present-tense verb negative, use **ei** followed by the verb without its personal ending. The form after **ei** is identical for all persons.
Affirmative | Negative
ma tea**n** | ma **ei** tea
sa räägi**d** | sa **ei** räägi
ta tööta**b** | ta **ei** tööta
me lähe**me** | me **ei** lähe
nad on | nad **ei** ole
The form after **ei** is the present-tense negative stem. Learn it alongside the dictionary form: **tegema — ei tee**, **minema — ei lähe**.
Ma ei tea.
translation: I don't know.

content: Ta ei tööta täna.
translation: He/she isn't working today.

content: Me ei lähe kinno.

content: Ma ei joo kohvi.

content: In negative clauses, a **direct object** normally takes the **partitive**: **Ma ei näe autot.** — I can't see the car. **Mul ei ole raha.** — I don't have any money. A subject or noun describing the subject does not change: **Ma ei ole arst.** — I'm not a doctor.
Incorrect: **Ma ei tean.** After **ei**, do not use a personal ending. Say **Ma ei tea.**
To say 'don't!' in an instruction, use **ära**, not **ei**: **Ära tule!** — Don't come! (See the lesson on the imperative.)
**Ma lähen sööma**, but **ma tahan süüa**. The preceding verb determines which infinitive you need.

Estonian verbs have two main infinitive forms. Dictionaries usually list the **-ma infinitive** (elama, sööma). The other is called the **-da infinitive**, although its ending can also be **-ta** or **-a** (elada, süüa).
-ma infinitive | -da infinitive | I (present) | Meaning
elama | elada | elan | to live
õppima | õppida | õpin | to study, learn
rääkima | rääkida | räägin | to speak, talk
ootama | oodata | ootan | to wait
tegema | teha | teen | to do, make
minema | minna | lähen | to go
tulema | tulla | tulen | to come
olema | olla | olen | to be
sööma | süüa | söön | to eat
jooma | juua | joon | to drink
nägema | näha | näen | to see
ostma | osta | ostan | to buy
You cannot always predict the **-da infinitive**. Learn three key forms together, such as **lugema — lugeda — loen**.
Use the -ma infinitive after these verbs
**minema** (to go and do something), **tulema** (to come and do something), **hakkama** (to start), **pidama** (to have to), **õppima** (to learn to do something).
Ma lähen poodi leiba ostma.
translation: I'm going to the shop to buy some bread.

content: Ma pean täna töötama.
translation: I have to work today.

content: Ma hakkan eesti keelt õppima.

content: Use the -da infinitive after these verbs and expressions

**tahtma** (to want), **võima** (may, to be allowed to), **saama** (to be able to), **oskama** (to know how to), **armastama** (to love doing something), **meeldima** (to like), **mul on vaja** (I need to).
Ma tahan süüa.
translation: I want to eat.

content: Many verbs form the simple past with **-si-**: ma elasin, sa elasid, ta elas. Negative: ma ei elanud.
Many Estonian verbs form the simple past with **-si-** (or just **-s** in the he/she form). Some common verbs have different stems or endings; learn them from the table below.
Person | Ending | elama — to live | rääkima — to speak
ma | -sin | ela**sin** | rääki**sin**
sa | -sid | ela**sid** | rääki**sid**
ta | -s | ela**s** | rääki**s**
me | -sime | ela**sime** | rääki**sime**
te | -site | ela**site** | rääki**site**
nad | -sid | ela**sid** | rääki**sid**
Common irregular verbs
Some high-frequency verbs have less predictable past-tense forms. They are worth learning by heart.
Verb | I (past) | he/she (past) | Negative past
olema — to be | olin | oli | ei olnud
minema — to go | läksin | läks | ei läinud
tulema — to come | tulin | tuli | ei tulnud
tegema — to do, make | tegin | tegi | ei teinud
nägema — to see | nägin | nägi | ei näinud
sööma — to eat | sõin | sõi | ei söönud
jooma — to drink | jõin | jõi | ei joonud
saama — to get | sain | sai | ei saanud
Past-tense negation
Use **ei** + the **-nud** form. The negative form is the same for every person: **ma ei elanud**, **nad ei elanud**.
Eile ma töötasin kodus.
translation: Yesterday I worked from home.

content: Some verbs use **-is** in the he/she past-tense form: **ta ostis** — he/she bought; **ta tahtis** — he/she wanted.
**Tule! — Tulge!** (Come! — Come! [plural/formal]) **Ära tule! — Ärge tulge!** (Don't come!)
**Informal singular 'you':** use the present-tense stem without its ending. Start with the 'I' form and remove **-n**: **tulen → tule!**, **räägin → räägi!**

**Plural or polite 'you':** use **-ge** or **-ke**. The **-da infinitive** provides a useful clue: if its ending is **-ta**, the imperative often ends in **-ke** (**oodata → oodake, võtta → võtke**). Otherwise, **-ge** is common (**rääkida → rääkige, tulla → tulge, süüa → sööge**). Learn frequent irregular forms such as **anda → andke, teha → tehke, näha → nähke**.
An important exception in the singular: **minema → ma lähen**, but the imperative is **mine!**, not **lähe!**
Verb | you (singular) | you (plural/formal)
tulema (tulla) | tule! | tul**ge**!
rääkima (rääkida) | räägi! | rääki**ge**!
istuma (istuda) | istu! | istu**ge**!
olema (olla) | ole! | ol**ge**!
minema (minna) | mine! | min**ge**!
ootama (oodata) | oota! | ooda**ke**!
vaatama (vaadata) | vaata! | vaada**ke**!
tegema (teha) | tee! | teh**ke**!
nägema (näha) | näe! | näh**ke**!
võtma (võtta) | võta! | võt**ke**!
andma (anda) | anna! | and**ke**!
sööma (süüa) | söö! | söö**ge**!
jooma (juua) | joo! | joo**ge**!
Negative commands
For a negative command, use **ära** (singular 'you') or **ärge** (plural/formal 'you') followed by the corresponding imperative verb form.
| Singular 'you' | Plural/formal 'you'
don't come | ära tule | ärge tulge
don't speak | ära räägi | ärge rääkige

content: Adjectives agree with the noun in the nominative plural: suur maja — suur**ed** maja**d**, uus auto — uu**ed** auto**d**.
**üks kohv**, but **kaks kohvi, viis eurot, palju aega**. Numbers and quantities often require the partitive.
After numbers **two and above**, the noun is normally in the **partitive singular** (the third main form), not the plural as in English. After **üks** (one), use the nominative singular.
One | Two or more
üks kohv | kaks kohv**i**
üks laps | kolm las**t**
üks euro | viis euro**t**
üks minut | kümme minuti**t**
üks kord | kaks kord**a**

After **mitu?** (how many?), also use the singular partitive: **mitu last?** After **palju** (a lot of), **vähe** (little/few), **natuke** (a little), and measurements such as **kilo**, **tass** and **pudel**, use the partitive, but choose singular or plural according to what you mean: mass nouns are usually singular (**palju vett, tass teed**), while countable nouns are often plural (**palju inimesi, kilo kartuleid**).
Üks kohv ja kaks teed, palun.
translation: One coffee and two teas, please.

content: Even when a compound number ends in **üks** (one), it takes a **partitive singular** noun: **kakskümmend üks raamatut** — twenty-one books.
**Ma joon kohvi. Ma armastan sind. Ma ei näe autot.** The object often takes the partitive case.

The **direct object** — the person or thing affected by an action — is often in the **partitive** (the third main form of the noun). Unlike English, Estonian marks many objects with a special case form.
Ma joon kohvi.
translation: I drink coffee. / I'm drinking coffee.

content: Use the **partitive** for objects in **negative sentences**: **Ma ei näe autot.** Some verbs also regularly require a partitive object, including **armastama** (to love), **ootama** (to wait for), and **aitama** (to help).

content: For a complete, finished action, an object can take a different case: **Ma ostsin raamatu.** — I bought the book. You'll learn this distinction at A2.
Adjectives come before the noun and agree with it: **suur maja** (big house), **suured majad** (big houses).
An adjective agrees with the noun it describes. In the **nominative plural**, the adjective also gets **-d**.
Singular | Plural
suur maja | suure**d** maja**d**
uus auto | uue**d** auto**d**
hea sõber | hea**d** sõbra**d**
väike laps | väikese**d** lapse**d**
With **olema** (to be), adjectives also agree with a plural subject.
Maja on suur. • Majad on suured.
translation: The house is big. • The houses are big.

content: Meil on uus korter.
translation: We have a new flat. / We have a new apartment.

content: In many other cases, both the adjective and the noun take the case ending: suure**s** maja**s** — in a big house. But with **-ga** (with/by), the ending is attached only to the last word: **uue autoga** — in a new car.
Ma elan suures majas.
translation: I live in a big house.

content: Ta sõidab uue autoga.
translation: He/she is travelling in a new car.

content: Incorrect: “Majad on suur.” The adjective must be plural: Majad on suur**ed**.
Estonian has 14 cases, but most follow familiar patterns: add an ending to the genitive stem, as in **raamatu-s** and **raamatu-ga**.

Estonian has **14 grammatical cases**. The first three — **nominative, genitive and partitive** — are the key forms to learn with each noun. Most other singular case forms are built from the genitive stem plus an ending. At A1, focus on the most common everyday uses. The book-based forms in the table illustrate the endings, even when the resulting expressions are uncommon in everyday speech.
Case (Estonian) | Question | Example | English meaning
nimetav (nominative) | kes? mis? | raamat | a book / the book
omastav (genitive) | kelle? mille? | raamatu | of the book / the book's
osastav (partitive) | keda? mida? | raamatu**t** | a book (as a partitive object)
sisseütlev (illative) | kuhu? millesse? | raamatu**sse** | into the book
seesütlev (inessive) | kus? milles? | raamatu**s** | in the book
seestütlev (elative) | kust? millest? | raamatu**st** | out of the book / about the book
alaleütlev (allative) | kellele? millele? | raamatu**le** | onto the book / to the book
alalütlev (adessive) | kellel? millel? | raamatu**l** | on the book
alaltütlev (ablative) | kellelt? millelt? | raamatu**lt** | off the book
kaasaütlev (comitative) | kellega? millega? | raamatu**ga** | with a book
ilmaütlev (abessive) | kelleta? milleta? | raamatu**ta** | without a book
saav (translative) | kelleks? milleks? | raamatu**ks** | into a book / as a book (result)
rajav (terminative) | milleni? | raamatu**ni** | as far as the book / up to the book
olev (essive) | kellena? millena? | raamatu**na** | as a book (in a role or state)
Mis on raamatus? • Ma räägin raamatust.
translation: What's in the book? • I'm talking about the book.

content: You do not need to memorise all 14 case names right away. Learn the question words instead: **kus?** (where?), **kuhu?** (where to?), **kust?** (where from?), **kellega?** (with whom?). They help you identify the case, although the exact word form still needs practice.
**Where? Where to? Where from?** Compare **poes — poodi — poest** and **tööl — tööle — töölt**.

Estonian uses two common sets of location endings. **Internal location** ('in/into/out of'): **-s** (where?), **-sse** (where to?), **-st** (where from?). **External location** ('on/onto/off', also at a place): **-l**, **-le**, **-lt**.
Place | Where? | Where to? | Where from?
kodu — home | kodu**s** | **koju** | kodu**st**
kool — school | kooli**s** | kooli | kooli**st**
pood — shop | poe**s** | poodi | poe**st**
linn — town, city | linna**s** | linna | linna**st**
Tallinn | Tallinna**s** | Tallinna**sse** | Tallinna**st**
Eesti | Eesti**s** | Eesti**sse** | Eesti**st**
töö — work | töö**l** | töö**le** | töö**lt**
turg — market | turu**l** | turu**le** | turu**lt**
pidu — party | peo**l** | peo**le** | peo**lt**
Saaremaa | Saaremaa**l** | Saaremaa**le** | Saaremaa**lt**
Short 'where to?' forms

Many common words have a short directional form without **-sse**: **kooli** (to school), **poodi** (to the shop), **linna** (into town), **majja** (into the house), **tuppa** (into the room), **kinno** (to the cinema), **koju** (home). Learn these forms as complete words.

translation: I live in Tallinn.

content: Memorise short destination forms such as **kooli, poodi, linna, koju**. Do not automatically add **-sse** to every place name.

Use **-l/-le/-lt** with many words for work, events, streets and islands: **tööl, peol, kontserdil, tänaval, Hiiumaal**. Some country names ending in **-maa** also take these endings: **Saksamaal** — in Germany.

content: kasutatud auto, joodav vesi, väsinud laps, tulev aasta — verb forms used like adjectives.

Participles describe people or things through an action, like “tired”, “boiled” or “growing”. Estonian has four main participles. You already know **-nud** and **-tud** from the perfect tense and the impersonal voice.
Form | Meaning | Example
**-v** | doing something | kasva**v** laps — a growing child
**-tav, -dav** | being done or able to be done | joo**dav** vesi — drinking water (drinkable water)
**-nud** | having done something or undergone a change | väsi**nud** laps — a tired child
**-tud, -dud** | something done to a person or thing | keede**tud** muna — a boiled egg
How to form participles
A common pattern: for **-v**, replace -ma with -v (elama → elav, tulema → tulev). For **-tav**, start from the impersonal past participle: -tud → -tav, -dud → -dav (tehtud → tehtav, söödud → söödav).
Verb | Active present participle | Impersonal present participle
tegema | tegev | tehtav
lugema | lugev | loetav
sööma | sööv | söödav
kasutama | kasutav | kasutatav
The -nud and -tud forms are the ones you know from the perfect tense and the impersonal voice: teinud, tehtud; lugenud, loetud; söönud, söödud.
Which participles change for case?

**-v** and **-tav** participles change for case and number like adjectives: tuleva**l** aasta**l** — next year. Before a noun, **-nud** and **-tud** participles do not change: möödunud nädala**l** — last week, keedetud kartulite**ga** — with boiled potatoes.

content: Many participles are used as ordinary adjectives: huvitav — interesting, tuntud — well-known, haritud — educated, armastatud — beloved, keelatud — forbidden, kadunud — missing.
Don't confuse -nud and -tud. **-nud** describes the one who did something: Ta on ukse avanud. — They have opened the door. **-tud** describes what was done: Uks on avatud. — The door is open.

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: The present and simple past (tehakse, tehti) are covered at A2. Compound tenses use **olema** + an impersonal past participle (**-tud/-dud**). In impersonal perfect and pluperfect constructions, olema stays in the third-person singular: on, oli.

content: Kõik piletid on juba müüdud.

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: Objects in the impersonal voice

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: A total object normally takes the nominative, not the genitive: **Uus kool** ehitati 2010. aastal. — A new school was built in 2010. A partial object still takes the partitive: **Kooli** ehitati kaks aastat. — The school was under construction for two years.

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: Action or state?

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: Form | Example

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: **suleti** — action | Pood suleti kell kuus. — The shop was closed at six.

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: **on suletud** — state | Pood on suletud. — The shop is closed.

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud

rule: Impersonal voice: on tehtud, oli tehtud
content: If you do not mean a particular “they”, use the impersonal form instead of Mulle ütlesid, et…: Mulle **öeldi**, et… — I was told that…
vaadates, lugedes, minnes — doing one thing while doing another.
The **-des** form often describes an action happening at the same time as the main action, usually performed by the same person. English often uses “while doing” or an -ing clause.
To form it, replace the final **-a** of the -da infinitive with **-es**.
-da infinitive | -des form
vaadata | vaadat**es**
lugeda | luged**es**
minna | minn**es**
tulla | tull**es**
teha | teh**es**
süüa | süü**es**
olla | oll**es**
Ta sööb telerit vaadates.
translation: They eat while watching TV.

content: Kodust lahkudes pane tuled kustu.
translation: Turn off the lights when leaving home.

content: Ma kuulan muusikat jalutades.
translation: I listen to music while walking.

content: Ta tuli koju lauldes.
translation: They came home singing.

content: Kodust lahkudes helistas mulle ema suggests that Mum was leaving home. If you were the one leaving, say: Kui ma kodust lahkusin, helistas mulle ema. — Mum called me when I left home.
Ta olevat haige. — Apparently, they're ill. The -vat form reports information from another source.
Extra topic. At B1, focus on recognising -vat in news and written texts rather than using it actively.

The **-vat** form (quotative mood) signals reported information without presenting it as the speaker's own firsthand knowledge. English often uses “apparently”, “reportedly” or “they say”. The form is the same for all persons: replace -ma with **-vat**.
Verb | Present | Past
olema | ole**vat** | olevat olnud
tulema | tule**vat** | olevat tulnud
minema | mine**vat** | olevat läinud
tegema | tege**vat** | olevat teinud
Negation: **ei** + the -vat form, e.g. ei tulevat, ei olevat tulnud.
Ta olevat haige.
translation: Apparently, they're ill.

content: Homme olevat ilus ilm.
translation: They say the weather will be nice tomorrow.

content: Rong olevat juba läinud.
translation: Apparently, the train has already left.

content: Ta ei tulevat täna tööle.
translation: Apparently, they won't be coming to work today.

content: Seal olevat väga hea restoran.
translation: There's reportedly a very good restaurant there.

content: In conversation, you can use simpler expressions: **Räägitakse, et** ta on haige. — They say they're ill. **Kuulsin, et** rong on juba läinud. — I heard the train had already left.
Don't confuse this with the -v participle: olev — existing, tulev — coming. The quotative form ends in **-vat**.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Homme sõidan Tartusse. Hakkan ujumas käima. Temast saab arst. — talking about the future without a future tense.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Estonian has no separate future tense. Use the **present tense** for future events, with context or time expressions such as homme (tomorrow), varsti (soon), järgmisel aastal (next year).

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Homme sõidan ma Tartusse.
translation: I'm going to Tartu tomorrow.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Ma helistan sulle õhtul.
translation: I'll call you this evening.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: hakkama + -ma

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: **hakkama** + the -ma infinitive means “start doing” or “begin to”. It highlights the start of an activity or a new habit.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Järgmisest kuust hakkan ma ujumas käima.
translation: I'll start going swimming next month.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Homme hakkan torti tegema.
translation: I'll start making the cake tomorrow.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Sügisel hakkab laps kooli minema.
translation: The child will start school in autumn.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Other expressions with future meaning

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: These are ordinary expressions that refer to the future, not separate future tense forms.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Expression | Example

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: **-st saab** — will become | Temast saab hea arst. — They'll make a good doctor.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: **tulema** — weather or events to come | Homme tuleb ilus ilm. — The weather will be nice tomorrow.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: **kavatsema** + -da — intend to | Ma kavatsen suvel Itaaliasse sõita. — I'm planning to go to Italy this summer.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: Don't automatically translate English “will be” as saama + olema. Ma saan olema homme kodus sounds unnecessarily heavy. Just say Ma **olen** homme kodus. The construction is possible (See saab olema põnev! — This is going to be exciting!), but is not a general future auxiliary.

rule: Talking about the future: hakkan tegema, tuleb
content: To highlight a future result, particles such as ära, valmis and läbi can help: Ma teen töö homseks valmis. — I'll finish the work by tomorrow.
Kui ma oleksin teadnud, oleksin tulnud. — If I had known, I would have come.
To talk about an unreal past situation, use the conditional of **olema** plus the **-nud** participle. English often uses “would have done” or “if … had done”.
Person | Affirmative | Negative
ma | oleksin teinud | ei oleks teinud
sa | oleksid teinud | ei oleks teinud
ta | oleks teinud | ei oleks teinud
me | oleksime teinud | ei oleks teinud
te | oleksite teinud | ei oleks teinud
nad | oleksid teinud | ei oleks teinud
Kui ma oleksin seda teadnud, oleksin varem tulnud.
translation: If I had known that, I would have come earlier.

content: Kui sa oleksid helistanud, oleksin sind aidanud.
translation: If you had called, I would have helped you.

content: Ma oleksin peaaegu bussist maha jäänud.
translation: I almost missed the bus.

content: Oleks tore olnud sind näha.
translation: It would have been nice to see you.

content: Sa oleksid pidanud mulle ütlema.
translation: You should have told me.

content: Compare: Kui mul **oleks** aega, ma **tuleksin**. — If I had time, I would come (now). Kui mul **oleks olnud** aega, ma **oleksin tulnud**. — If I had had time, I would have come (then).
Short forms are also common: ma oleks teinud, me oleks läinud. The negative **poleks** means ei oleks.
Ma muudan plaani. — Plaan muutub. One verb changes something, the other describes something changing.

In many verb pairs, one verb takes a direct object (transitive), while the other describes what happens to the subject without a direct object (intransitive). English often uses the same verb for both: “I open the door” and “The door opens”.
With an object | Without an object / related meaning
muutma — change something | muutuma — change, become different
alustama — start something | algama — begin, start
lõpetama — finish something | lõppema — end
avama — open something | avanema — open up
sulgema — close something | sulguma — close, shut
parandama — repair, improve something | paranema — recover, improve
arendama — develop something | arenema — develop, evolve
kasvatama — raise, grow something | kasvama — grow
tõstma — raise, lift something | tõusma — rise, get up
peatama — stop something | peatuma — come to a stop
rahustama — calm someone | rahunema — calm down
õpetama — teach | õppima — learn, study (can also take an object)
Kontsert algab kell seitse.
translation: The concert starts at seven.

content: Me alustame koosolekut kell seitse.
translation: We're starting the meeting at seven.

content: Hinnad tõusevad iga aastaga.
translation: Prices rise every year.

content: Ta tõstis käe.
translation: They raised their hand.

content: Ma õpetan oma vennale eesti keelt.
translation: I teach my brother Estonian.

content: Ilm on paranenud.
translation: The weather has improved.

content: Another useful pair: **kaotama** — lose (Ma kaotasin võtmed. — I lost my keys) and **kaduma** — disappear (Võtmed kadusid. — The keys disappeared).

For the change-of-state pairs above, ask whether the subject acts on something else or undergoes the change itself. This is a useful guide, not a rule for every verb (õppima, for example, can take an object).
Tund lõpetab kell kolm is not the right way to say the lesson ends at three. Say Tund **lõpeb** kell kolm. But: Ma **lõpetan** töö kell kolm. — I finish work at three.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Ta sai arstiks. Läks pimedaks. Ta värvis toa siniseks. — expressing change with -ks.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: The **-ks** ending (translative case) often describes a new role, state or result: what someone **becomes**, or what someone **makes** something become.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Verb | Example

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **saama** — become | Ta sai õpetajaks. — They became a teacher.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **minema** — become, get (state or weather) | Läks pimedaks. — It got dark.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **jääma** — become, remain | Ta jäi haigeks. — They fell ill.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **muutuma** — become, change | Ilm muutus soojaks. — The weather became warm.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **tegema** — make something a certain way | See uudis tegi mind õnnelikuks. — This news made me happy.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **värvima** — paint | Ta värvis toa siniseks. — They painted the room blue.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **valima** — elect, choose | Ta valiti klassivanemaks. — They were elected class representative.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Becoming someone: -st saab

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: When talking about what someone will become, you can also use **-st saab**. The person undergoing the change is in the elative (-st).

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Temast saab meie uus ülemus.
translation: They'll be our new boss.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Mis sinust suurena saab?
translation: What will you be when you grow up?

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Remaining and leaving something in a state

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **jääma** means remain or end up in a state; **jätma** means leave something in a state. These verbs often occur in fixed expressions without -ks. Learn the expressions as a whole.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Uks jäi lahti.
translation: The door stayed open.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Jäta uks lahti, palun.
translation: Please leave the door open.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Me jäime hotelliga rahule.
translation: We were satisfied with the hotel.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Ära jää hiljaks!
translation: Don't be late!

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Expressions with jääma. With -ks: haigeks jääma — fall ill, hiljaks jääma — be late. Other fixed expressions: magama jääma — fall asleep, rahule jääma — be satisfied, vait jääma — fall silent, ellu jääma — survive.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: **rikki minema** — break down or go bad: Telefon läks rikki. — The phone broke. Soojas läheb toit kergesti rikki. — Food spoils easily in warm conditions. For food, you can also say **halvaks minema** or **riknema**.

rule: Becoming and changing things: -ks with verbs
content: Don't say Ta töötab õpetajaks. Use -ks for becoming something and -na (essive) for working or acting as something: Ta sai õpetaja**ks** — they became a teacher; Ta töötab õpetaja**na** — they work as a teacher (see the A2 topic on -ks and -na).

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: ära sööma, läbi lugema, valmis tegema, kokku leppima — verb particles change the meaning of a verb.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: You may already know particle verbs such as aru saama and üles tõusma from A2. Many particles have recurring meanings. Learning these can help you understand unfamiliar combinations, although some need to be learnt as whole expressions.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Particle | Common meaning | Example

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: ära | completion; away | ära sööma — eat up, ära minema — go away

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: läbi | all the way through | läbi lugema — read through, finish reading

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: valmis | until ready | valmis tegema — finish making

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: üles | up | üles kirjutama — write down

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: maha | down; behind | maha kukkuma — fall down

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: välja | out; off | välja mõtlema — think up, välja lülitama — switch off

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: sisse | in; on | sisse lülitama — switch on

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: kokku | together | kokku leppima — agree on something

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: üle | again, review | üle vaatama — look over

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: järele | reflect; after | järele mõtlema — think it over

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: edasi / tagasi | forward / back | edasi lükkama — postpone

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: **ära** is a very common particle. It often marks completion (ära sööma — eat up), in which case a total object is common if the quantity is also bounded. Sometimes it changes the whole meaning (ära minema — leave, ära unustama — forget). Learn these combinations as units.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Kes jõi minu kohvi ära?
translation: Who drank my coffee?

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Ma unustasin selle ära.
translation: I forgot about it.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Ootame vihma ära.
translation: Let's wait for the rain to pass.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Vaata tekst veel kord üle!
translation: Look over the text once more!

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Me leppisime kokku, et kohtume reedel.
translation: We agreed to meet on Friday.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Mõtle järele!
translation: Think it over!

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Koosolek lükati edasi.
translation: The meeting was postponed.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: A particle can change the meaning completely: **minema** — go, **ära minema** — leave; **jääma** — stay, **maha jääma** — miss (a bus, train), fall behind; **pidama** — have to, **vastu pidama** — withstand, hold out.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: In a simple main clause, the particle often follows the finite verb: Ma lülitan arvuti välja. With -ma and -da infinitives, it normally comes before the verb: Ma pean arvuti välja lülitama. The order can vary with emphasis and sentence structure.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Process or result?

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Object case depends on whether the action is ongoing or covers a bounded object and reaches a result (see the A2 topic on total and partial objects). A particle often signals a result, but the meaning of the whole sentence determines the case.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: Meaning | Example

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: process — partitive (osastav) | Ma loen raamatut. — I'm reading a book.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: completed result — total object | Ma lugesin raamatu läbi. — I read the whole book.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: negation — partitive (osastav) | Ma ei lugenud raamatut läbi. — I didn't finish the book.

rule: Verb particles: ära, läbi, valmis, üles…
content: If you mean you finished reading the whole book, don't say Ma lugesin raamatut läbi. Use a total object: Ma lugesin **raamatu** läbi.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest, keskenduma millele, osalema milles — verbs that require a particular case.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Building on the A2 topic on verbs and cases, learn more fixed verb patterns. English prepositions don't always match Estonian endings. Learn each verb together with the question and case it requires (also called verb government).

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: sõltuma — depend on | millest? (elative) | See sõltub ilmast. — It depends on the weather.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: loobuma — give up | millest? (elative) | Ta loobus suitsetamisest. — They gave up smoking.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: hoolima — care about | kellest? millest? (elative) | Ma hoolin sinust. — I care about you.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: keskenduma — focus on | millele? (allative) | Keskendu tööle! — Focus on your work!

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: osalema — take part in | milles? millel? (inessive/adessive) | Ma osalen projektis. — I'm taking part in a project.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: nõustuma — agree with | kellega? millega? (comitative) | Ma nõustun sinuga. — I agree with you.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: kahtlema — doubt, be unsure about | milles? (inessive) | Ma kahtlen selles. — I doubt it.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: uskuma — believe, believe in | keda? mida? millesse? (partitive/illative) | Ma ei usu seda. — I don't believe it.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: tänama — thank | keda? mille eest? | Tänan teid abi eest! — Thank you for your help!

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: õnnitlema — congratulate | keda? mille puhul? | Õnnitlen sind sünnipäeva puhul! — Happy birthday!

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: vastutama — be responsible for | mille eest? | Kes selle eest vastutab? — Who is responsible for this?

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: kuuluma — belong to | kellele? (allative) | See auto kuulub minu vennale. — This car belongs to my brother.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: eelistama — prefer | mida? millele? (partitive/allative) | Ma eelistan teed kohvile. — I prefer tea to coffee.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: muretsema — worry about | kelle pärast? | Ära muretse minu pärast! — Don't worry about me!

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: paluma — ask for | kellelt? mida? (ablative/partitive) | Ma palusin temalt abi. — I asked them for help.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: huvi tundma — be interested in | mille vastu? | Ta tunneb huvi ajaloo vastu. — They're interested in history.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Forgetting or leaving something: where to?

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: When you say where you forgot, left or put something, Estonian normally uses a destination form answering **kuhu?** (where to?), even when English uses “at”, “in” or “on”.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Ma unustasin võtmed koju.
translation: I left my keys at home.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Jätsin vihmavarju bussi.
translation: I left my umbrella on the bus.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Kuhu sa auto parkisid?
translation: Where did you park your car? (Estonian uses kuhu? — where to?)

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Don't say Ma unustasin võtmed kodus when you mean you left the keys at home. Say Ma unustasin võtmed **koju**.

rule: Verb case patterns: sõltuma millest, loobuma millest…
content: Remember aitama (help): use **keda?** (partitive), not kellele? (allative): Ma aitan **sind**. — I'll help you.
selles uues majas, nende uute majadega — adjectives and demonstratives follow the noun's case and number.
Adjectives, demonstratives (see, too, need) and ordinal numbers normally agree with the noun in case and number. There are four important case exceptions below.
Case / question | Singular | Plural
nominative (kes? mis?) | see uus maja | need uued majad
genitive (kelle? mille?) | selle uue maja | nende uute majade
partitive (keda? mida?) | seda uut maja | neid uusi maju
inessive (kus?) | selles uues majas | nendes uutes majades
illative (kuhu?) | sellesse uude majja | nendesse uutesse majadesse
comitative (kellega? millega?) | selle uue majaga | nende uute majadega
The endings **-ni, -na, -ta, -ga** (terminative, essive, abessive and comitative) go on the final noun. Its agreeing modifiers take the genitive instead: selle uue maja**ga**, ilma sooja jope**ta**.
Pane õunad suurde sinisesse kasti.

rule: Cause, purpose and concession: selleks et, seetõttu
content: A comma separates the subordinate clause. With multiword conjunctions such as selleks et, sellepärast et, enne kui and juhul kui, the comma usually comes before the whole conjunction, but it can come between its parts depending on meaning and emphasis: Õpin eesti keelt, selleks et tööd leida. • Õpin eesti keelt selleks, et tööd leida.
Ta ütles, et tuleb homme. Ta küsis, kas mul on aega. Ta palus mul helistada.

Use **et** to report a statement, **kas** for a yes/no question, or the original question word. Unlike English, Estonian does not normally backshift tenses just because the reporting verb is in the past. Choose the tense according to the meaning. Adjust pronouns and time or place expressions if the viewpoint changes (täna → sel päeval, homme → järgmisel päeval). If reporting on the same day, täna can stay: “Ma tulen täna.” → Ta ütles, et tuleb täna. — They said they were coming today.
Direct speech | Reported speech
«Ma olen väsinud.» | Ta ütles, et ta on väsinud.
«Ma olin haige.» | Ta ütles, et ta oli haige.
«Kas sul on aega?» | Ta küsis, kas mul on aega.
«Millal sa tuled?» | Ta küsis, millal ma tulen.
«Helista mulle!» | Ta palus, et ma talle helistaksin. • Ta palus mul talle helistada.
To report requests or advice, use **et + conditional** or **kellel? (adessive) + -da**, for example with paluma, soovitama and käskima.

content: For an indirect yes/no question, translate English “if” or “whether” as **kas**, not kui: Ta küsis, **kas** mul on aega. — They asked if I had time.
esiteks, lisaks, aga, vaid, näiteks, seega, kokkuvõttes — words that connect ideas.
In B1 writing and speaking tasks, link your ideas clearly. These words help you put ideas in order, add information, contrast points, give examples and draw conclusions.
Purpose | Connectors
sequence | esiteks, teiseks; kõigepealt, siis, seejärel, lõpuks — firstly, secondly; first of all, then, after that, finally
addition | lisaks (sellele), peale selle, samuti, ka, ning — in addition (to that), besides, likewise, also, and
contrast | aga, kuid, vaid, seevastu, teisalt — but, however, but rather, in contrast, on the other hand
example | näiteks — for example
conclusion | seega, niisiis, seetõttu, kokkuvõttes — therefore, so, for that reason, in summary
Paired conjunctions
Pair | Example
nii … kui ka — both … and | Ta räägib nii eesti kui ka vene keelt. — They speak both Estonian and Russian.
kas … või — either … or | Tule kas täna või homme. — Come either today or tomorrow.
ei … ega — neither … nor | Ma ei joo kohvi ega teed. — I drink neither coffee nor tea.
mitte ainult …, vaid ka — not only … but also | Ta ei ole ainult õpetaja, vaid ka kirjanik. — They're not only a teacher but also a writer.

ühelt poolt …, teiselt poolt — on the one hand … on the other hand | Ühelt poolt on linnas mugav, teiselt poolt on seal kallis. — On the one hand, living in the city is convenient; on the other, it's expensive.
aga or vaid?

Use **vaid** to correct a negated idea: Ma ei ela Tallinnas, vaid Tartus. — I don't live in Tallinn, but in Tartu. Use **aga** or **kuid** to contrast two ideas: Ma ei ela Tallinnas, aga töötan seal. — I don't live in Tallinn, but I work there.

content: Don't use aga to replace a negated item in Ma ei ela Tallinnas, aga Tartus. Use **vaid**: Ma ei ela Tallinnas, vaid Tartus.

A sentence-initial connector often takes the finite verb next: Seega **on** meil… • Lisaks **tahan** ma öelda… Coordinating conjunctions such as aga, kuid and ning do not themselves trigger inversion: Aga ma **tahan**…

Kas te saaksite…? Kas oleks võimalik…? Ma soovitaksin… — polite language using the conditional.
The conditional mood (covered at A2) can soften a request. At B1, practise making requests, suggestions, giving advice and declining politely.

request | Kas te saaksite…? • Kas te võiksite…? • Palun… — Could you…? / Would you…? / Please…

content: A direct command like Andke mulle kohvi! (Give me coffee!) can sound abrupt. More polite: Kas ma saaksin kohvi? — Could I have some coffee? Or simply Üks kohv, palun. — One coffee, please.
When addressing one person formally in a letter, you may capitalise **Teie**, **Teile** and **Teid** as a mark of respect. See the topic on letters and notices.
How to open and close a letter, when to write Teie, and how to write a notice — useful skills for B1 writing tasks.

Practise two common B1 writing task formats: a short text of around 50 words (message, notice or questionnaire answers) and a longer text of around 100 words (letter or narrative). A letter should include a greeting, the reason for writing, relevant details and a closing. Follow the word limit and instructions in your actual task.
| Personal letter | Formal letter
greeting | Tere, Mari! • Kallis Jüri! | Lugupeetud härra Tamm! • Tere!
opening sentence | Aitäh kirja eest! • Kuidas sul läheb? | Kirjutan Teile, et… • Pöördun Teie poole seoses…
closing | Tervitades • Kallistan • Kõike head! | Lugupidamisega • Parimate soovidega
Punctuation

After a greeting, use an exclamation mark or no final punctuation: **Tere, Mari!** Put a comma between Tere and the name. Unlike English, Estonian does **not** put a comma after closing phrases such as **Tervitades** (Best wishes) or **Lugupidamisega** (Kind regards). Write your name on the next line.
When writing formally to one person, **Teie**, Teile and Teid may traditionally be capitalised as a sign of respect. When addressing several people, use lowercase **teie**.
Writing a notice
Keep a notice brief: what happened or will happen, where and when, what the reader should do, and how to contact you. For example, a message telling colleagues you will leave work early:
Homme lahkun töölt juba kell 14.

triibuline, naljakas, uskumatu, ebamugav, kolmeaastane — use word parts to work out the meaning of adjectives.
Building on the A2 topic on suffixes, these word-building patterns help you recognise and form adjectives.
Affix | Meaning | Example
-line | having a feature, pattern or characteristic | triibu**line** — striped, lille**line** — floral
-ne | having a certain amount or age (among other uses) | kolmeaasta**ne** — three-year-old
-kas | having a quality; somewhat | nalja**kas** — funny, sina**kas** — bluish
-lik | having a quality or characteristic | vaja**lik** — necessary, rahu**lik** — calm
-tu | without, lacking | rahu**tu** — restless, õnne**tu** — unhappy
-matu | un-, not done or not possible (from verbs) | usku**matu** — unbelievable, unusta**matu** — unforgettable
eba- | un-, in-, dis- (opposite meaning) | **eba**mugav — uncomfortable, **eba**viisakas — impolite
Number + noun + -line or -ne: kahetoaline korter — a two-room flat, viieminutiline paus — a five-minute break, kolmeaastane laps — a three-year-old child.
Shades of colour
**hele-** means light, **tume-** means dark, and **-kas** can mean -ish: helesinine — light blue, tumepunane — dark red, rohekas — greenish.

content: The suffix -tu often attaches to a noun (töö → töötu — unemployed), while -matu forms adjectives from verbs (uskuma → uskumatu — unbelievable, väsima → väsimatu — tireless).
kogemus, tulemus, kunstnik, perekond, sõnastik, sõbranna — noun suffixes and compound words.
At this level, recognising these suffixes matters more than inventing new words yourself. They can help you work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word.
Suffix | Meaning | Example
-us | abstract concept, action or result | lahendama → lahend**us** — solution, harjutama → harjut**us** — exercise
-mus | outcome or experience | kogema → koge**mus** — experience, tulema → tule**mus** — result, elama → ela**mus** — memorable experience
-nik | person associated with an activity or role | kunst → kunst**nik** — artist, amet → amet**nik** — official
-kond | group or collective | pere → pere**kond** — family, mees → mees**kond** — team
-stik | collection or system | sõna → sõna**stik** — dictionary, mägi → mäe**stik** — mountain range
-nna | female person | sõber → sõbra**nna** — female friend, kuningas → kuninga**nna** — queen
Compound words

The **last** part of a typical compound noun tells you what the thing is, and the first part describes it. The first noun is often in the genitive: raamatu|pood — bookshop (raamatu — of a book), laste|aed — kindergarten (laste — of children). Usually only the last part changes for case: raamatupoe**s**, lasteaia**s**.
